tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

  - targetPort updated to 80 to match both deployments’ container port

- Pods:
  - Stable: 2 pods (version=v2.0) Running
  - Canary: 2 pods (version=v2.1) Running

Notes:

- Session affinity is None, so distribution should be fairly even across endpoints.

If you want to tweak weighting without additional tooling, you can adjust replica counts (e.g., 3 stable, 1 canary ≈ 75/25). To instantly roll back traffic to stable only, set the Service selector back to app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.0 or scale canary to 0.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

- Deployed canary Deployment:
  - Name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80, same security configuration as stable (no special securityContext specified, matching engine-v2-0)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to route ~50/50:
  - Selector now matches app: recommendation-engine (targets both stable v2.0 and canary v2.1)
  - targetPort updated to 80 to match both deployments’ container port

Validation:
- Pods:
  - Stable: 2 pods (version=v2.0) Running
  - Canary: 2 pods (version=v2.1) Running
- Service Endpoints now include all 4 pods on port 80, so traffic will spread roughly 50/50 across stable and canary.

Notes:
- Previously, the Service targeted port 8080, while the deployments expose port 80. I adjusted Service targetPort to 80 to correctly route traffic to both versions.
- Session affinity is None, so distribution should be fairly even across endpoints.

If you want to tweak weighting without additional tooling, you can adjust replica counts (e.g., 3 stable, 1 canary ≈ 75/25). To instantly roll back traffic to stable only, set the Service selector back to app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.0 or scale canary to 0.

results.taskOutput:
Done. Your pod is now Running.

What happened
- Root cause: The pod needed PVC homepage-pvc with storageClass “sc”, but that StorageClass doesn’t exist. The pod stayed Pending with message: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

- Recreated homepage-pvc using storageClass: standard and the same size (1Gi).

- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to volume pvc-4e157518-7f40-441e-bf21-1f9a845b2b14.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, container Ready=true.

If you intended to use a different StorageClass name, let me know the correct one and I can recreate the PVC accordingly.

Done. Your pod is now Running.

What happened
- Root cause: The pod needed PVC homepage-pvc with storageClass “sc”, but that StorageClass doesn’t exist. The pod stayed Pending with message: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”
- Available StorageClasses in the cluster: standard (default), csi-hostpath-sc.

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC (it wasn’t bound, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc using storageClass: standard and the same size (1Gi).
- The PVC was dynamically provisioned and Bound, allowing the pod to schedule and start.

- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to volume pvc-4e157518-7f40-441e-bf21-1f9a845b2b14.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080 (not 80), and your probes pointed to non-existent paths on port 80 (/is_ready and /get_status). This made the pod “Running” but not “Ready”, so the Service had no healthy endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 (metadata) and kept 80 as non-functional metadata is harmless.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready (webapp-7d8467cb84-qmzlv)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080 (healthy)

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then browse http://localhost:8080 or curl http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route yet. I can create one if you tell me the host you want to use (e.g., webapp.example.com).

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080 (not 80), and your probes pointed to non-existent paths on port 80 (/is_ready and /get_status). This made the pod “Running” but not “Ready”, so the Service had no healthy endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080 (metadata) and kept 80 as non-functional metadata is harmless.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: 8080.

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Ready (webapp-7d8467cb84-qmzlv)
- Service endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080 (healthy)

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get pods
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then browse http://localhost:8080 or curl http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There is no Ingress/Route yet. I can create one if you tell me the host you want to use (e.g., webapp.example.com).

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1), not pods.
- Pods are in the core API group (""), so the SA lacked permissions to list them.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Left the existing deployments list permission as-is.

Verification commands (run any of these)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- The permission applies only to the simple-rbac-setup namespace via the Role/RoleBinding you have. If you need pod access in other namespaces, create equivalent Role/RoleBinding there or use a ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1), not pods.
- Pods are in the core API group (""), so the SA lacked permissions to list them.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Left the existing deployments list permission as-is.

Verification commands (run any of these)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- The permission applies only to the simple-rbac-setup namespace via the Role/RoleBinding you have. If you need pod access in other namespaces, create equivalent Role/RoleBinding there or use a ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1), not pods.
- Pods are in the core API group (""), so the SA lacked permissions to list them.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Left the existing deployments list permission as-is.

Verification commands (run any of these)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- The permission applies only to the simple-rbac-setup namespace via the Role/RoleBinding you have. If you need pod access in other namespaces, create equivalent Role/RoleBinding there or use a ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints were attached to the Service (EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints).
- The Service targeted the wrong container port:
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (name: http)
- After the change, the EndpointSlice shows the pod endpoint and port 8080.

Verification
- EndpointSlice now populated with endpoint 10.244.0.26 and port 8080.
- Launched a temporary curl pod and tested:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned HTTP 200
  - nc to nginx:80 succeeded

How you can validate
- Check the Service:
  - kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
  - kubectl -n web get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=nginx -o wide
- Test from a pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl-term --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
  - kubectl -n web exec -it curl-term -- sh -lc "curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/"
  - Expect 200

Notes
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if supported): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress or OpenShift Route pointing to Service nginx:80.

Optional cleanup
- Remove test pods:
  - kubectl -n web delete pod curl-term curl-test toolbox

Current status: The nginx Service in namespace web is now accessible within the cluster on port 80 (targeting container port 8080) and returns HTTP 200.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints were attached to the Service (EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints).
- The Service targeted the wrong container port:
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (name: http)
- After the change, the EndpointSlice shows the pod endpoint and port 8080.

Verification
- EndpointSlice now populated with endpoint 10.244.0.26 and port 8080.
- Launched a temporary curl pod and tested:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned HTTP 200
  - nc to nginx:80 succeeded

How you can validate
- Check the Service:
  - kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
  - kubectl -n web get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=nginx -o wide
- Test from a pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl-term --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
  - kubectl -n web exec -it curl-term -- sh -lc "curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/"
  - Expect 200

Notes
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if supported): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress or OpenShift Route pointing to Service nginx:80.

Optional cleanup
- Remove test pods:
  - kubectl -n web delete pod curl-term curl-test toolbox

Current status: The nginx Service in namespace web is now accessible within the cluster on port 80 (targeting container port 8080) and returns HTTP 200.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Pod/Deployment labels: app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints were attached to the Service (EndpointSlice initially had no endpoints).
- The Service targeted the wrong container port:
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have hit the wrong port.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (name: http)
- After the change, the EndpointSlice shows the pod endpoint and port 8080.

Verification
- EndpointSlice now populated with endpoint 10.244.0.26 and port 8080.
- Launched a temporary curl pod and tested:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned HTTP 200
  - nc to nginx:80 succeeded

How you can validate
- Check the Service:
  - kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
  - kubectl -n web get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=nginx -o wide
- Test from a pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl-term --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
  - kubectl -n web exec -it curl-term -- sh -lc "curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local/"
  - Expect 200

Notes
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
  - LoadBalancer (if supported): kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress/Route: create an Ingress or OpenShift Route pointing to Service nginx:80.

Optional cleanup
- Remove test pods:
  - kubectl -n web delete pod curl-term curl-test toolbox

Current status: The nginx Service in namespace web is now accessible within the cluster on port 80 (targeting container port 8080) and returns HTTP 200.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to a scheduling constraint. The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label.
- As a result, both pods were Pending (FailedScheduling) and the service had no endpoints, which led to connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I did
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.
- Verified rollout:
  - 2 pods are now Running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-bnkkc, web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-p778v.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.31:80, 10.244.0.32:80.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods available.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints present and pointing to the running pods.

Why this fixes it
- With pods running and ready, kube-proxy can route traffic from the ClusterIP to the backing pod IP:port, so connections to web-app-service on port 80 should now succeed.

Recommended follow‑ups
- If you intended to pin this workload to specific nodes:
  - Either label an appropriate node and reintroduce nodeSelector (e.g., kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Adjust the selector to match actual node labels you use in this cluster.
- Update your Git/manifest source of truth. The Deployment’s last-applied-configuration still contained the old nodeSelector; re-applying that manifest would reintroduce the problem. I can provide an updated manifest if you use GitOps.

Optional verification (quick checks)
- From any pod in the namespace: curl -sS web-app-service:80 or curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 to confirm 200 OK.
- If your frontend app still reports errors, share its pod name and logs and I’ll trace requests end-to-end.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reapply a Deployment with a corrected nodeSelector/tolerations, or
- Label specific nodes to satisfy the original placement intent.

namespace/webshop-frontend created

deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to a scheduling constraint. The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label.
- As a result, both pods were Pending (FailedScheduling) and the service had no endpoints, which led to connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I did
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.
- Verified rollout:
  - 2 pods are now Running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-bnkkc, web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-p778v.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.31:80, 10.244.0.32:80.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods available.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints present and pointing to the running pods.

Why this fixes it
- With pods running and ready, kube-proxy can route traffic from the ClusterIP to the backing pod IP:port, so connections to web-app-service on port 80 should now succeed.

Recommended follow‑ups
- If you intended to pin this workload to specific nodes:
  - Either label an appropriate node and reintroduce nodeSelector (e.g., kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Adjust the selector to match actual node labels you use in this cluster.
- Update your Git/manifest source of truth. The Deployment’s last-applied-configuration still contained the old nodeSelector; re-applying that manifest would reintroduce the problem. I can provide an updated manifest if you use GitOps.

Optional verification (quick checks)
- From any pod in the namespace: curl -sS web-app-service:80 or curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 to confirm 200 OK.
- If your frontend app still reports errors, share its pod name and logs and I’ll trace requests end-to-end.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reapply a Deployment with a corrected nodeSelector/tolerations, or
- Label specific nodes to satisfy the original placement intent.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Pods were not running due to a scheduling constraint. The Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label.
- As a result, both pods were Pending (FailedScheduling) and the service had no endpoints, which led to connection refused when resolving web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local.

What I did
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.
- Verified rollout:
  - 2 pods are now Running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-bnkkc, web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-p778v.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.31:80, 10.244.0.32:80.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods available.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints present and pointing to the running pods.

Why this fixes it
- With pods running and ready, kube-proxy can route traffic from the ClusterIP to the backing pod IP:port, so connections to web-app-service on port 80 should now succeed.

Recommended follow‑ups
- If you intended to pin this workload to specific nodes:
  - Either label an appropriate node and reintroduce nodeSelector (e.g., kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu), or
  - Adjust the selector to match actual node labels you use in this cluster.
- Update your Git/manifest source of truth. The Deployment’s last-applied-configuration still contained the old nodeSelector; re-applying that manifest would reintroduce the problem. I can provide an updated manifest if you use GitOps.

Optional verification (quick checks)
- From any pod in the namespace: curl -sS web-app-service:80 or curl -sS web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 to confirm 200 OK.
- If your frontend app still reports errors, share its pod name and logs and I’ll trace requests end-to-end.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reapply a Deployment with a corrected nodeSelector/tolerations, or
- Label specific nodes to satisfy the original placement intent.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to enforce multi‑tenancy and least privilege.

What I created
- Namespaces
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Service accounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- RBAC
  - Each developer user gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-users -> alice, dev-bob/rb-admin-users -> bob, dev-charlie/rb-admin-users -> charlie (ClusterRole admin)
  - Each developer SA gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-sa -> alice-sa, dev-bob/rb-admin-sa -> bob-sa, dev-charlie/rb-admin-sa -> charlie-sa (ClusterRole admin)
  - Read-only to dev-shared for users and SAs:
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-users -> alice, bob, charlie (ClusterRole view)
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-sas -> alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa (ClusterRole view)
  - No developer access granted to staging or prod (only cluster-admins can access those by default)
- ResourceQuotas
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi mem, 10 pods, 5 services
  - dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi mem, 20 pods, 10 services
  - staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi mem, 50 pods, 20 services
- NetworkPolicies (default deny + explicit allows)
  - Default deny all ingress/egress in each of: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
  - Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
  - Allow egress to DNS/system services (kube-system, ports 53/udp,53/tcp,443,6443) in every namespace
  - Dev namespaces:
    - Allow egress to dev-shared
    - Allow ingress from dev-shared
    - No cross-developer communication (only same-namespace + dev-shared permitted)
  - dev-shared:
    - Allow ingress from and egress to dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
  - staging/prod:
    - Isolated from dev namespaces: only same-namespace traffic allowed, plus DNS/system egress

Notes and assumptions
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-Kubernetes). If your cluster CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicies, isolation won’t take effect.
- DNS/service access is permitted by selecting kube-system namespace and standard DNS ports. If your cluster DNS runs elsewhere or your API server needs to be reachable via egress policy, adjust the namespaceSelector or add an IPBlock for the API server endpoint as needed.
- We did not grant any RBAC in staging/prod; cluster-admins still have access via their clusterrolebinding (system:masters), while developers have none there.

How to verify (quick checks)
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice      (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice (no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice         (no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - Try curl/ping between pods in different dev namespaces (should fail), same namespace (should work), to dev-shared (should work)

Service account tokens (if needed)
- Kubernetes 1.24+: create short-lived token:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

If you want me to tweak DNS/system egress for a different DNS namespace or to explicitly allow API server access via IP/CIDR, tell me your environment details and I’ll adjust the policies.

arguments.resource:
# Namespaces
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-alice
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-bob
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-charlie
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: charlie
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    env: dev
    role: shared
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod

# Service Accounts (per developer namespace)
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

# ResourceQuotas
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-developer-namespace
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-developer-namespace
  namespace: dev-bob
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-developer-namespace
  namespace: dev-charlie
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-dev-shared
  namespace: dev-shared
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 8Gi
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-stage-prod
  namespace: staging
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"
---
apiVersion: v1

metadata:
  name: rq-stage-prod
  namespace: prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "50"
    services: "20"

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to enforce multi‑tenancy and least privilege.

What I created
- Namespaces
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Service accounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- RBAC
  - Each developer user gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-users -> alice, dev-bob/rb-admin-users -> bob, dev-charlie/rb-admin-users -> charlie (ClusterRole admin)
  - Each developer SA gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-sa -> alice-sa, dev-bob/rb-admin-sa -> bob-sa, dev-charlie/rb-admin-sa -> charlie-sa (ClusterRole admin)
  - Read-only to dev-shared for users and SAs:
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-users -> alice, bob, charlie (ClusterRole view)
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-sas -> alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa (ClusterRole view)
  - No developer access granted to staging or prod (only cluster-admins can access those by default)
- ResourceQuotas
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi mem, 10 pods, 5 services
  - dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi mem, 20 pods, 10 services
  - staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi mem, 50 pods, 20 services
- NetworkPolicies (default deny + explicit allows)
  - Default deny all ingress/egress in each of: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
  - Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
  - Allow egress to DNS/system services (kube-system, ports 53/udp,53/tcp,443,6443) in every namespace
  - Dev namespaces:
    - Allow egress to dev-shared
    - Allow ingress from dev-shared
    - No cross-developer communication (only same-namespace + dev-shared permitted)
  - dev-shared:
    - Allow ingress from and egress to dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
  - staging/prod:
    - Isolated from dev namespaces: only same-namespace traffic allowed, plus DNS/system egress

Notes and assumptions
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-Kubernetes). If your cluster CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicies, isolation won’t take effect.
- DNS/service access is permitted by selecting kube-system namespace and standard DNS ports. If your cluster DNS runs elsewhere or your API server needs to be reachable via egress policy, adjust the namespaceSelector or add an IPBlock for the API server endpoint as needed.
- We did not grant any RBAC in staging/prod; cluster-admins still have access via their clusterrolebinding (system:masters), while developers have none there.

How to verify (quick checks)
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice      (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice (no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice         (no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - Try curl/ping between pods in different dev namespaces (should fail), same namespace (should work), to dev-shared (should work)

Service account tokens (if needed)
- Kubernetes 1.24+: create short-lived token:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

If you want me to tweak DNS/system egress for a different DNS namespace or to explicitly allow API server access via IP/CIDR, tell me your environment details and I’ll adjust the policies.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to enforce multi‑tenancy and least privilege.

What I created
- Namespaces
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Service accounts
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- RBAC
  - Each developer user gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-users -> alice, dev-bob/rb-admin-users -> bob, dev-charlie/rb-admin-users -> charlie (ClusterRole admin)
  - Each developer SA gets admin in their own namespace:
    - RoleBindings: dev-alice/rb-admin-sa -> alice-sa, dev-bob/rb-admin-sa -> bob-sa, dev-charlie/rb-admin-sa -> charlie-sa (ClusterRole admin)
  - Read-only to dev-shared for users and SAs:
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-users -> alice, bob, charlie (ClusterRole view)
    - RoleBinding dev-shared/rb-view-sas -> alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa (ClusterRole view)
  - No developer access granted to staging or prod (only cluster-admins can access those by default)
- ResourceQuotas
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPU, 4Gi mem, 10 pods, 5 services
  - dev-shared: 4 CPU, 8Gi mem, 20 pods, 10 services
  - staging/prod: 8 CPU, 16Gi mem, 50 pods, 20 services
- NetworkPolicies (default deny + explicit allows)
  - Default deny all ingress/egress in each of: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
  - Allow same-namespace traffic in each namespace
  - Allow egress to DNS/system services (kube-system, ports 53/udp,53/tcp,443,6443) in every namespace
  - Dev namespaces:
    - Allow egress to dev-shared
    - Allow ingress from dev-shared
    - No cross-developer communication (only same-namespace + dev-shared permitted)
  - dev-shared:
    - Allow ingress from and egress to dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie
  - staging/prod:
    - Isolated from dev namespaces: only same-namespace traffic allowed, plus DNS/system egress

Notes and assumptions
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-Kubernetes). If your cluster CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicies, isolation won’t take effect.
- DNS/service access is permitted by selecting kube-system namespace and standard DNS ports. If your cluster DNS runs elsewhere or your API server needs to be reachable via egress policy, adjust the namespaceSelector or add an IPBlock for the API server endpoint as needed.
- We did not grant any RBAC in staging/prod; cluster-admins still have access via their clusterrolebinding (system:masters), while developers have none there.

How to verify (quick checks)
- Namespaces:
  - kubectl get ns dev-alice dev-bob dev-charlie dev-shared staging prod
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice      (yes)
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice (no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice         (no)
- Quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- NetworkPolicies:
  - kubectl get networkpolicy -n dev-alice
  - Try curl/ping between pods in different dev namespaces (should fail), same namespace (should work), to dev-shared (should work)

Service account tokens (if needed)
- Kubernetes 1.24+: create short-lived token:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

If you want me to tweak DNS/system egress for a different DNS namespace or to explicitly allow API server access via IP/CIDR, tell me your environment details and I’ll adjust the policies.
